KEY MESSAGE 1...

Latest water vapor imagery shows a deep fetch of moisture
streaming from the Gulf and western Atlantic northward into the
Northeast ahead of an amplifying shortwave trough tracking
into the Saint Lawrence River Valley. There is good consensus
that the trough starts to take on a negative tilt towards 12 UTC
and with a jet streak strengthening over the Northeast, strong
lift and upper level divergence overlapping such a moisture 
rich environment will help amplify rainfall rates across eastern
NY and western New England through early this morning. Forecast soundings 
also show the classic tall/skinny CAPE profile with high 
freezing heights supporting efficient warm rain processes and 
potential for high rainfall rates across the region. Latest 
HREF shows a southwest to northeast oriented ribbon of medium to
high probabilities for 3-hrly rainfall amounts from 09 to 15 
UTC exceeding 1" focused in the mid-Hudson Valley into NW CT and
New England. There is even low probabilities for over 2" of 
rain in a 3-hr period during this window. This matches the 
slight risk (level 2 of 4) Day 1 ERO placement and will feature
the highest chance for high rainfall rates to result in 
isolated to scattered instances of flash flooding. They also 
show a veering wind profile with south to southwesterly winds 
extending through a deep layer with small corfidi vectors 
indicating potential for backbuilding heavy rainfall early this 
morning. While the mid- Hudson Valley into NW CT and parts of 
western MA missed out on the extreme rainfall from last week, 
the risk for flash flooding will nonetheless increase should 
heavy rainfall rates persist over a given area. Luckily, the 
incoming trough will limit the duration of the high rainfall 
rates and help shift it further into New England by 15 - 18 UTC,
decreasing the potential for widespread flash flooding issues. 
Total rainfall amounts through 15 UTC Monday across eastern NY 
and western New England from the latest HREF PMM guidance shows 
potential for 0.5 to 2 inches with locally higher amounts likely
where heavy rain can persist.

After the main area of widespread rain exits into New England by
mid-morning, we enter into a brief break before the main trough
axis and sfc cold front swings through from west to east by 15 -
21 UTC. Should sufficient breaks of sun or thinning of cloud
coverage occur, the environment will destabilize further. CAMs
are in good agreement with a line of convection developing 
ahead of the sfc boundary and tracking eastward through the
afternoon. Strong low-level convergence ahead of the front will
help focus moisture and lift, likely supporting additional 
periods of heavy rain. Areas that have already become saturated
from the overnight/early morning rainfall will be more 
vulnerable to localized flooding but given the progressive
nature of the front and any convection, any additional flooding
should be isolated/localized.


KEY MESSAGE 2...

There looks to be a small window of opportunity from mid-
morning through early to mid afternoon for clouds to thin enough
or even briefly break for insolation. Given the very moist 
environment including dew points in the upper 60s to even low 
70s today, any insolation will easily contribute to increased 
sfc-based instability with CAMs showing 1000 - 2000J/kg 
developing mainly along and east of the Hudson River into 
western New England where there should a longer delay before the
front arrives. Strong dynamics/lift ahead of the negatively 
tilted trough will support strong southerly winds through the 
column with veering winds in the low-levels also supporting 
directional shear. This favors a high shear, low/modest CAPE 
environment with the latest guidance in good agreement with 
impressive deep layer shear amounts ranging 40 to 50kts ahead of
the boundary. This can easily support organized convection and 
allow updrafts to grow upscale, should instability be 
sufficient. The latest probabilities for strong 2-5km updraft 
helicity values from the HREF are rather low at only 10-20% as 
the front pushes through this afternoon suggesting the 
atmosphere may not have enough time to destabilize between the 
exiting heavy rain and incoming convective line. However, the 
impressive shear and strong dynamics aloft are reasons to 
maintain a watchful eye on thunderstorms through this afternoon
even if they remain low topped as they can still become strong 
to severe and produce damaging winds should any updrafts become 
tall enough. The SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook continues to show 
the marginal risk (level 1 of 5) from Hudson River eastward into
western New England but now includes a low chance (2%) chance 
for an isolated tornado given low-level directional shear and 
veering winds.
